newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asian Metals - Aluminium slide lures Japan buying.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals - Aluminium slide lures Japan buying.

text.p: A continued slide in London Metal Exchange aluminium prices to fresh two-and-a-half-year lows early this week lured some Japanese end users to the market, although buying was modest and consumers remained unconvinced the market had found a floor, traders said on Wednesday.

"There's some buying, but it's not such great volume and it's focused on nearby delivery," said one Japanese trader. "There's still no confirmation that (prices) won't fall further, so it's hard to buy forward."
LME benchmark three-month aluminium slid on Monday to a low of $1,387 a tonne and retested that level on Tuesday before bouncing back to $1,400.
The recovery was partly in sympathy with copper, which surged following the announcement of a large 8,825-tonne drop in LME warehouse stocks.

One trader said $1,350 would probably be the next big number for LME aluminium to be watched by Japanese consumers. He estimated they probably still had to fill nearly half of their fourth-quarter needs.

Japan's physical aluminium premiums remained stable at recent levels, while the latest data for Yokohama warehouse stocks showed a rise to nearly 240,000 tonnes at the end of August from previous levels of about 200,000 tonnes.
One trader played down the increase in stock, however, saying: "It's just trade house positions."
Looking ahead at Japan's aluminium demand, Sky Aluminium Co chief executive Kenichi Watanabe expected only lukewarm growth of one or two percent, including exports, this year and next.
He told a news conference on Wednesday that cool weather at the end of this summer would weigh on production and sales of beverage can sheet in the second half of this year.
Sky is Japan's fourth-largest producer of aluminium sheet.
In the copper market, traders said physical tightness continued to ease gradually and premiums softened, although activity was dull.
"Generally speaking, the only good market right now is the U.S.," said one trade house source.

He said Sumitomo Corp's announcement last week that the trading house saw its losses from unauthorised copper trading as larger than previously estimated offered no major surprise to the market, which had largely put the scandal behind it.

Japanese traders said after the announcement that, while it was unclear whether some institutions may still be holding large positions taken over from Sumitomo, the market was now focusing more on supply-and-demand factors.
Sumitomo officials said last Thursday that the company had liquidated most of the unauthorised long positions it blamed for its estimated $2.6 billion loss.
However, they declined to comment on the size of the positions they had liquidated, how they were liquidated or in whose hands they may now be held.

In the zinc market, traders noted that despite talk of GSP-related buying from China last month by Japanese smelters at premiums of $100 a tonne over LME, business was quiet and premiums remained at a notional $70 to $90 a tonne.
